projects.title: OSINT World Monitor
projects.description: Self-hosted intelligence platform collecting from 69 data sources — news, conflict records, satellite fire detections, military aircraft. Computes a country stress index, backtests its own predictions, and publishes where they fail. Runs on a Raspberry Pi 5.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content: Open-source intelligence tools either cost thousands per seat or require you to trust a third party with your queries. News aggregators show headlines but don't cross-reference them against satellite data, conflict records, or market movements. I wanted a system that collects public data from every domain — geopolitical events, disasters, markets, cyber threats, fire detections, military aircraft — normalises it into one shape, and puts it on a map with the provenance attached. Everything local. Nothing leaves the machine.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.content: 69 data sources feed into a Python/FastAPI backend. 14 core fetchers (GDELT, ACLED, USGS, NASA FIRMS, ADS-B, Polymarket, and more) plus 55 RSS feeds from outlets across 4 ownership classes. Celery workers handle scheduled ingestion. PostgreSQL stores everything with a 30-day retention lifecycle that trims its own oldest data. The frontend is a Next.js console with an interactive world map, filterable by domain, severity, and time range. Ollama runs locally for LLM-powered situation summaries and story gists. The entire stack runs on a single Raspberry Pi 5 (8GB).

sections.title: Key Technical Decisions
sections.content: Every computed number carries a method_version string and is pre-registered before any output is inspected. The composite country stress index combines geopolitical, market, hazard, and wildfire domain signals — weights are fixed at ¼ each. Corroboration scoring tracks how many independent outlets cover the same event, distinguishing genuine cross-source confirmation from syndicated rewrites. Story clustering uses ownership metadata to prevent related outlets from inflating corroboration counts.

sections.title: What Was Tested
sections.content: The composite index was evaluated against ACLED-derived ground truth labels across 3 pre-registered protocols: incidence evaluation (can the score distinguish high-event months?), onset evaluation (can it detect new escalations?), and within-country evaluation (does a country's own score predict its own future?). Labels define armed conflict onset (≥10 battle fatalities/week), mass protest escalation (≥20 demonstrations AND ≥5 riots/week), and state-based violence intensification (2× monthly fatality increase with ≥25 floor). Positive rates: 26.5% train, 21.8% held-out test.

sections.title: What Failed — and Why That Matters
sections.content: The composite scored AUROC 0.502 on incidence (barely above coin-flip), 0.496–0.526 on onset (no predictive power), and failed the within-country test entirely. The held-out test set confirmed: the score dominates nothing. These results are published in the repository, not hidden. The system is honest about what it can and cannot do — it is a monitoring tool that shows evidence, not an oracle that predicts futures. Publishing failures is the point: a system that only reports successes is not doing science.

sections.title: What I Learned
sections.content: Pre-registration is the difference between measurement and storytelling — without it, you can always find a metric that makes your system look good. Running ML on constrained hardware (8GB Pi) forces real engineering trade-offs: model selection matters when you can't just throw GPU at the problem. And the hardest part of building an intelligence system isn't the code — it's deciding what counts as ground truth.

projects.title: Raspberry Pi Homelab
projects.description: Two-board homelab running production infrastructure. Board one handles OSINT data collection under Docker Compose. Board two is a k3s Kubernetes cluster hosting nine services: Jellyfin, Vaultwarden, Immich, Kiwix, Uptime Kuma, ArchiveBox, and more. Custom fleet dashboard built with raw Node.js (no framework). 1TB SSD + 6TB HDD, Tailscale mesh networking with real TLS certificates.

sections.title: The Setup
sections.content: Board one (pi) runs Docker Compose handling the OSINT data collection pipeline — PostgreSQL, Celery workers, and the Next.js console. Board two (pi2) runs a k3s Kubernetes cluster hosting nine services: Jellyfin for media, Vaultwarden for passwords, Immich for photos, Kiwix for offline Wikipedia, Uptime Kuma for monitoring, ArchiveBox for web archiving, and more. A custom fleet dashboard built with raw Node.js (no framework) shows the health of everything.

sections.title: Storage Philosophy
sections.content: Two rules, and everything else follows from them. First: a drive is a folder. Open a board's share and you see its drives, named for what they are. Nothing that is not a drive sits beside them. Second: the split is by how a file is read, not by what it is called. Anything read at random — settings, databases, caches, artwork — lives on the SSD. Anything you'd recognise as a file — films, .zim archives, downloads — lives on the 6TB HDD. A database is called data and behaves like an app: Jellyfin's library index is 50MB and thousands of tiny seeks, and on a spinning disk it makes the whole interface feel slow.

sections.title: Networking
sections.content: Tailscale mesh networking connects both boards with real TLS certificates — every service is accessible from any device on the tailnet without port forwarding or exposing anything to the public internet. Each service gets its own tailnet hostname (jellyfin.tailnet.ts.net, vault.tailnet.ts.net, etc.) and any can be installed as a standalone app from a browser.

sections.title: Deployment
sections.content: Everything deploys from the Mac, never from the Pi. A Makefile drives it: make bootstrap for first-time board setup, make dashboard-k8s for the fleet dashboard, make media for Jellyfin and Kiwix, make vault for Vaultwarden. Node agents run on each board — Glances for system metrics plus a Pi-specific shim for power draw and CPU throttle state. The build log, storage layout, and dashboard data contract are all documented in the repo.

sections.title: What I Learned
sections.content: Running production services on 8GB of RAM forces you to care about resource allocation in a way that cloud infrastructure never does. Every container's memory limit matters. k3s is genuinely production-ready on ARM — the only pain point is the occasional container image that doesn't publish an arm64 build. The fleet dashboard exists because every monitoring tool I tried consumed more resources than the services it was monitoring. And three earlier attempts at organising storage each made the same files reachable by two paths at once, which is what a duplicate is — simplicity won.

projects.title: Market Intelligence Platform
projects.description: Bloomberg Terminal on a budget. Processes 500 to 1,000 financial articles daily from 100+ sources using FinBERT sentiment analysis (90% accuracy). Features a custom Geopolitical Risk Index, TF-IDF story clustering, and a Hindsight Validator that backtests sentiment predictions against real market returns. Cut LLM API costs 80% by running BERT locally.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content: Bloomberg Terminal costs $24,000 a year. News aggregators show headlines but don't tell you what they mean — no sentiment scoring, no entity extraction, no cross-source clustering. If you want intelligence, not just information, you either pay enterprise prices or build it yourself.

sections.title: The Pipeline
sections.content: Four layers. Layer 1 ingests from NewsAPI, RSS feeds (Reuters, Bloomberg, BBC, CNN), and GDELT's global events database — roughly 500-1,000 articles per day after deduplication. Layer 2 enriches every article: FinBERT scores sentiment (-1 to +1 with confidence), compromise.js extracts named entities, and a weighted formula calculates impact from sentiment strength, cluster size, source credibility, and recency. Layer 3 clusters stories using TF-IDF and sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), then threads them across days so you can follow a developing situation. Layer 4 surfaces the intelligence: a custom Geopolitical Risk Index, sentiment timelines per entity, and a Hindsight Validator that backtests past predictions against actual market movements.

sections.title: Local-First Architecture
sections.content: Most AI news platforms send every article to expensive LLM APIs. This pipeline runs FinBERT, NER, and TF-IDF locally — the heavy lifting happens on-device. LLMs (Gemini) are used only for high-value synthesis like executive briefings. Result: 80% cost reduction compared to an API-first approach, plus faster processing since there's no network round-trip for the core analysis.

sections.title: The Hindsight Validator
sections.content: The most honest feature. It takes past sentiment predictions and checks them against what actually happened in the market. Did a negative sentiment spike on a company actually precede a stock drop? The validator shows the correlation — or the lack of it. No system that only shows wins is trustworthy.

sections.title: What I Learned
sections.content: Source credibility weighting matters more than model accuracy — a perfect classifier on unreliable sources produces unreliable intelligence. Clustering is harder than classification because there's no ground truth for what constitutes 'the same story.' And local-first ML is viable for production: FinBERT on a CPU handles the throughput without any GPU infrastructure.

projects.title: HomeForge
projects.description: A private cloud you can run at home in one command. Deploys 15+ services (AI chat, file storage, messaging, VPN) using Docker-in-Docker for zero-dependency installation. Built zero-trust secret derivation with HKDF-SHA512, encrypted storage with SQLCipher, and custom TOTP 2FA with BIP39 recovery. Three-tier network segmentation keeps services isolated.

projects.title: Budgeting Schedule Automation
projects.description: Replaces Excel master budgets with a logic-based engine. Links 13 financial schedules from sales forecasts through to the budgeted balance sheet and cash flow. When one number changes, every downstream schedule recalculates automatically. Reduced processing time from 240 minutes to 24 minutes (90% reduction).
